title: Metallic Bonds
objective: After this level you can explain why metals conduct electricity and bend without breaking.
summary: In a metal, outer electrons roam as a sea around positive ions. Free electrons carry current, and a hammered metal's layers slide but stay bonded, while salt's shifted layers shatter.

cards.headline: Hit a metal bar with a hammer and it dents. Hit a salt crystal and it shatters.
cards.body: Both are held together by electrical attraction. So why does one bend and the other break? The answer is where the electrons go.

cards.headline: A sea of electrons
cards.body: In a metal, the atoms pack tightly and let their outermost electrons go. Those electrons don't belong to any one atom, or even any one pair. They wander through the whole piece, a sea of electrons around positive metal ions, and that shared sea holds the metal together: the metallic bond. Salt trades electrons, water shares them in pairs, and metals pool them.
cards.callout: Metallic bond: positive ions in a shared sea of electrons

cards.headline: Why electricity flows through metal
cards.body: Those free electrons are also why metals conduct electricity so well: the electrons can move, so a current can flow through the metal. Solid salt can't do this, because its ions are locked in place. Melt it or dissolve it, and the ions can move and carry a current.

cards.headline: Bend, don't break
cards.body: Hammer a metal and its layers of ions slide past each other. The electron sea simply flows along, keeping everything bonded, so the metal flattens instead of cracking. Shift the layers of a salt crystal and ions of the same charge end up side by side. They repel, and the crystal shatters. Same hammer, opposite fates.

cards.headline: Metallic bonds: pooled
learned: Metals pool their outer electrons in a shared sea
Free electrons let metals conduct electricity
Metal layers slide but stay bonded, so metals bend
Ionic crystals shatter when like charges meet

questions.prompt: In a metallic bond, where are the metal atoms' outer electrons?

options.label: Shared in a sea that moves through the whole metal
Paired up between exactly two neighboring atoms
options.rationale: That's a covalent bond; metal electrons roam freely.

options.label: Handed over for good to form a grid of ions
options.rationale: That's the ionic trade in salt.

options.label: Stripped off and lost into the surrounding air
options.rationale: They stay in the metal, just not tied to any one atom.

questions.explanation: In a metal, the outer electrons wander through the whole piece as a sea around positive metal ions.

questions.prompt: Why can an electric current flow through a metal wire?

options.label: Its ions are locked in a rigid grid
options.rationale: Locked ions are why solid salt doesn't conduct.

options.label: Its atoms share electrons only in pairs
options.rationale: Paired electrons stay put; metals' free electrons move.

options.label: Its free electrons can move through the metal
It contains salt dissolved in water
options.rationale: A solid metal wire conducts on its own.

questions.explanation: A metal's outer electrons are free to move, so they can carry a current through it.

questions.prompt: Level 43's salt and a metal are both held by electrical attraction. Why does salt shatter when struck while the metal bends?

options.label: Salt has no bonds holding it together at all
options.rationale: Salt's ionic bonds are strong: it melts only at 801 °C.

options.label: Shifted salt layers push like charges together
Metal atoms are much softer than salt ions
options.rationale: It's the bonding, not softness of atoms.

options.label: Salt is secretly a liquid inside its crystal
options.rationale: Salt is a solid grid of ions.

questions.explanation: Shift salt's grid and ions of the same charge meet and repel, so it shatters. A metal's electron sea keeps sliding layers bonded.
